beats.narration_text: Ciao — this is Liam. Episode 6 of 6. The casebook is an argument, not a collection. Five files go into the submission. Each file makes one claim. The claims build. The last check before you submit is a honesty pass on every 'actual outcome' line in every case — because if any of those lines contain the system's reported artifact instead of an independently verified world state, the entire argument fails at its foundation. Four minutes.

beats.act: the five-file set — what each file claims
beats.narration_text: Five files. First: the system dossier, named zero-zero-dossier.md. This was your entry ticket from Episode 1. It describes what the system is — the six fields: system name, access method, tool surface, blast radius, authorization statement, and the prediction-lock you wrote before any trial. It makes one claim: here is what I agreed to audit and what I expected to find. Second: the case files, one per case. Named with the Case ID you chose in the case template. Each makes one claim: here is what I observed when I applied this lens under these conditions. Third: failure-statistics.md. This file makes one claim: here is a structured tally of my findings, divided by fundamental and contingent. Fourth: attestation.md. This file makes one claim: here is exactly what I tested, what I did not test, and who owns each remaining gate — attested with calibrated verbs. Fifth: go-no-go.md. This file makes one claim: given my evidence, this is my calibrated recommendation for what should happen to this system next. Five files. Five claims. They build in order. A reviewer should be able to read them sequentially and reconstruct your entire argument without asking you any questions.

lines: Each file makes one claim — they build in order

beats.narration_text: The failure-statistics.md file requires a distinction the rubric will check: fundamental versus contingent failures. A contingent failure is one that could be fixed without redesigning the system. A bug in the stop-condition logic. A configuration parameter set incorrectly. A training data refresh that would resolve the base-rate anchor. Contingent failures can be remediated — the fix exists in principle, even if it has not been applied. A fundamental failure is one that cannot be fixed without redesigning the system at an architectural level. If the fairness impossibility theorem shows that the system's architecture simultaneously satisfies demographic parity and therefore cannot satisfy equal opportunity — that is not a bug. That is a mathematical property of the architecture. It cannot be patched away. If the system's stop condition is the only signal available to it — it cannot query the underlying resource because it has no access — then agentic false-success is not a bug; it is a design constraint. Fundamental failures determine the memo's verb more than contingent ones do. A single fundamental failure with High severity pushes toward refuse. Multiple contingent failures with Medium severity push toward modify. Name each failure in your tally as fundamental or contingent, explain why, and let that classification drive the go/no-go verb.

lines: The classification that drives the go/no-go verb
Fundamental: cannot be fixed without redesigning the architecture. Mathematical property. Design constraint.

beats.act: 'what would change my mind' — the paragraph that proves the argument is honest
beats.narration_text: The casebook closes with a paragraph called 'what would change my mind.' This paragraph earns points not by showing how much you found — but by showing that you understand the limits of what you found. The paragraph names: the specific evidence that would cause you to change your go/no-go verb, and the direction of the change. Two forms. If your verb is refuse or modify, the 'what would change my mind' paragraph names what would move you toward deploy: 'If a third-party audit found no agentic false-success cases under concurrent multi-user load conditions — the conditions I could not test — and if the system owner documented an independent verification path for the stop condition, I would revisit the verb to modify or deploy.' If your verb is deploy, the paragraph names what would move you toward modify or refuse: 'If the system's demographic leverage on variable X proves to be greater than my single-case measurement suggested — specifically, if a multi-case study found output deltas exceeding Y — I would revise the verb to modify.' The paragraph is not a hedge. It is a demonstration that your recommendation is grounded in evidence, not certainty — and that you know exactly what evidence is missing. That is the difference between a verdict and an honest audit.

lines: The paragraph that proves the argument is honest
Names: the specific evidence that would change your go/no-go verb
Verb = refuse/modify / what would move you toward deploy: named

beats.act: final honesty pass — check every actual-outcome line
beats.narration_text: Before you submit, run a single final check. Open every case file. Read Field 7 — actual outcome — in every case. Ask yourself: how do I know this? If the answer is 'the system told me' or 'the success message said' or 'the confirmation email arrived,' stop. That is not the actual outcome. That is the reported artifact from Field 6. The actual outcome requires an independent observation: you queried the underlying resource after the action, you checked a log that the system itself does not control, you observed the downstream state through a channel the system cannot manipulate. If any actual-outcome line in any case is sourced only from the system's own report, you have a fabricated case — not fabricated intentionally, but epistemically fabricated: you accepted the artifact as the world. Rewrite it. Describe what you actually observed about the world state, and if you cannot because you did not check, note it as an unverified actual outcome and demote the severity accordingly. A casebook with honest uncertainty is worth more points than a casebook with confident fabrication. Fabricated output — including a fabricated actual-outcome field — is zero for that case. Check the field. Verify the source. Then submit.

lines: One question per case: how do I know this?
F7 requires independent observation: query resource / check log outside system

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Assemble and Ship. The casebook is five files, each making one claim, building in order. System dossier: what you agreed to audit. Case files: what you observed. Failure statistics: fundamental versus contingent tally, driving the go/no-go verb. Attestation: what tested, what not tested, who clears which gate, calibrated verbs. Go/no-go memo: calibrated verb plus named use plus named owner plus stop condition. The 'what would change my mind' paragraph proves the argument is bounded by evidence — name the specific evidence that would shift the verb and in which direction. The final honesty pass is not optional: read every actual-outcome line, ask how you know it, and rewrite any line that is sourced from the system's own report. A casebook that knows its limits is a casebook that earns points. A casebook that mistakes the artifact for the world is the thing this entire course was built to prevent.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the final prompt — run it with all five file components ready in context. The prompt reads: I am assembling my Agentic Casebook for submission. I have the following files attached: 00-dossier.md, my three or more case files, failure-statistics.md, attestation.md, and go-no-go.md. Run the following checks. First: read every actual-outcome line in every case file. For each, tell me whether the evidence source is the system's own report or an independent observation. Flag any line that is sourced from the system's report and suggest how to rewrite it. Second: check that failure-statistics.md has a fundamental versus contingent classification for each failure and that the classifications are consistent with the go/no-go verb. Third: confirm the 'what would change my mind' paragraph is present, names specific evidence, and names the direction of verb change. Fourth: scan the attestation for any verb that is stronger than the evidence the cases support. Flag it. After the check, give me a pass/fail on each of the four checks and a list of any items I need to fix before submitting. End quote. Fix everything flagged. Then submit. The casebook is an argument. Send it when the argument is honest.
